games.title: Hack
games.note: Written by Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School students after they were refused Rogue's source code.

games.title: NetHack
games.note: Mike Stephenson, Izchak Miller and Janet Walz grew it from Hack's code; it is still being updated decades later.

games.title: Moria (1983)
games.note: Written at the University of Oklahoma; its town-above-a-dungeon design later shaped Diablo.

games.title: Angband
games.note: Two University of Warwick students built it from UMoria's code; Diablo began as a turn-based game modeled on it.

games.title: Ancient Domains of Mystery
games.note: Better known as ADOM; Thomas Biskup started it at the Technical University of Dortmund.

games.title: Torneko's Great Adventure: Mystery Dungeon
games.note: A Dragon Quest spin-off that brought Rogue-style dungeons to consoles and started the Mystery Dungeon series.

games.title: Shiren the Wanderer
games.note: The first Mystery Dungeon game with its own hero; English-speaking players first got it as a 2008 DS remake.

games.title: Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Red Rescue Team
games.note: Released alongside Blue Rescue Team on the DS; you play as a Pokémon on a rescue team.

games.title: Linley's Dungeon Crawl
games.note: Linley Henzell began programming it in 1995; its community continuation became Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup.

games.title: Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup
games.note: Darshan Shaligram and Erik Piper started it in 2006 to restart Crawl's development; it is free and playable in a browser.

games.title: Telengard
games.note: A deep, randomly stocked dungeon crawl; David Brevik named it among Diablo's influences.

games.title: Dwarf Fortress
games.note: In development since 2002; a paid Steam edition with graphics arrived in December 2022.

games.title: Minecraft
games.note: Markus Persson released the first public version in May 2009; it became the best-selling video game of all time.

games.title: Spelunker
games.note: Tim Martin's 1983 Atari game; Irem's 1985 arcade and Famicom versions made it a cult favorite in Japan.

games.title: La-Mulana
games.note: A Japanese freeware homage to MSX-era games, released in June 2006; Nigoro remade it for WiiWare in 2011.

games.title: Rick Dangerous
games.note: Core Design's trap-filled Indiana Jones pastiche, made years before the studio's Tomb Raider.

games.title: Spelunky
games.note: Released free for Windows in December 2008; an enhanced remake came to Xbox Live Arcade in July 2012.

games.title: UFO 50
games.note: Fifty original games for an imaginary 1980s console, made by six developers including Derek Yu and Ojiro Fumoto.

games.title: Downwell
games.note: Ojiro Fumoto's thirteenth game-a-week project, started after reading a Gamasutra article by Rami Ismail.

games.title: The Binding of Isaac
games.note: McMillen expected it to flop and barely tested it; it sold over a million copies in its first year.

games.title: The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth
games.note: A rebuilt remake that escaped the original's Flash limits and brought the game to consoles.

games.title: Super Meat Boy
games.note: Edmund McMillen and Tommy Refenes made it as a two-person team; its success let McMillen gamble on The Binding of Isaac.

games.title: Desktop Dungeons
games.note: A South African puzzle-roguelike built around ten-minute dungeons; a freeware version came first, then a 2013 remake.

games.title: Smash TV
games.note: A violent future game show where contestants blast through rooms for prizes, using Robotron-style twin joysticks.

games.title: Robotron: 2084
games.dev: Vid Kidz (Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar) / Williams
games.note: One joystick moves and the other shoots, a scheme Eugene Jarvis returned to in Smash TV.

games.title: Mewgenics
games.note: Shelved by Team Meat in 2016, then finished by McMillen and Glaiel; it sold a million copies in its first week.

games.title: FTL: Faster Than Light
games.dev: Subset Games (Jay Ma and Matthew Davis)
games.note: Two former 2K Shanghai developers asked Kickstarter for $10,000 and raised about $200,000.

games.title: Weird Worlds: Return to Infinite Space
games.note: Short, randomized space voyages; FTL's designers named it as an influence.

games.title: Into the Breach
games.note: Jay Ma cited Pacific Rim and Man of Steel, where whole cities get wrecked, when making buildings worth protecting.

games.title: Rogue Legacy
games.dev: Cellar Door Games (Teddy and Kenny Lee)
games.note: Each death hands the castle to an heir with random traits such as color blindness or dwarfism.

games.title: Dungeons of Dredmor
games.note: A comedic roguelike that Rogue Legacy's Teddy Lee named among his main inspirations.

links.took: Rogue's random dungeons, letter-coded monsters and permadeath, rewritten from scratch.
links.added: Freely shared code that others kept extending; that openness led to NetHack.
links.extra: Jay Fenlason and fellow Lincoln-Sudbury students met Rogue at UC Berkeley and were refused its source code.

links.took: Hack's source code: its dungeon, monsters and items.
links.added: Years of additions by an online DevTeam, known for anticipating almost anything a player tries.

links.took: Rogue's randomly generated levels and permanent death.
links.added: A town with shops above a deep Tolkien-themed dungeon, ending with the Balrog.
links.extra: Robert Alan Koeneke wrote it at the University of Oklahoma, inspired by both Adventure and Rogue.

links.took: UMoria's source code, Jim Wilson's version of Moria.
links.added: A much deeper dungeon of Tolkien monsters, ending with Morgoth instead of the Balrog.
links.extra: Built by Alex Cutler and Andy Astrand at the University of Warwick.

links.took: Concepts from NetHack: its items, monsters and interlocking rules.
links.added: A story-driven world with quests and creeping chaos corruption, designed to be less complex.
links.extra: Thomas Biskup said Rogue and Hack inspired him, NetHack in particular, though its complexity put him off.

links.took: Rogue's random dungeons, turn-based steps and harsh losses on death.
links.added: A friendlier console version starring Dragon Quest's merchant Torneko.

src.t: Iwata Asks: Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Gates to Infinity, Nintendo

links.extra: Koichi Nakamura said the aim was a more understandable, easier-to-play Rogue for consoles.

links.took: Torneko the merchant, plus Dragon Quest monsters and items.
links.added: Randomly generated dungeons in place of a scripted quest.

links.took: Chunsoft's Mystery Dungeon rules: random floors, hunger and turn-based fights.
links.added: An original wandering hero in a Japanese-inspired land and a longer, tougher journey.

links.took: The Mystery Dungeon formula, which Tsunekazu Ishihara admired as a game you could play a thousand times.
links.added: You play as a Pokémon on a rescue team, with a partner and story missions.

src.t: Iwata Asks: Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Gates to Infinity, Nintendo

links.extra: In Iwata Asks, The Pokémon Company's Ishihara says Torneko's game inspired him to pair Pokémon with Mystery Dungeon.

links.took: Pokémon species, types and moves.
links.added: A turn-based dungeon crawler with randomly generated floors.

links.took: Playing as a Pokémon on a rescue team through Mystery Dungeon floors.
links.added: A new story about time and a larger roster, on the DS.

links.took: Rogue popularized turn-based, permadeath dungeon crawling drawn in text characters.
links.added: Many playable species, gods to worship and branching dungeons.

links.took: Crawl's code and design, picked up after Linley Henzell stopped development.
links.added: Community-led removal of tedium, tile graphics, browser play and an auto-travel command.

links.took: Dungeon levels that persist between visits, as in NetHack.
links.added: A travel command for crossing explored levels, built on borrowed pathfinding code.

links.took: Randomly generated levels and a stricter penalty for death than most games.
links.added: Real-time mouse-driven combat, gothic graphics and online play through Battle.net.

src.t: GamesBeat, How Diablo found inspiration in hockey, Star Wars, and X-Com (David Brevik)

links.extra: David Brevik discovered Rogue in college.

links.took: A single town with a few shops above an endless, randomly generated dungeon.
links.added: Real-time action and a gothic horror atmosphere.

src.t: David Brevik via GameBanshee, The Making of Diablo, 2010

links.extra: Brevik named Moria and Warcraft as the biggest influences, and called Moria a big influence on the core structure.

links.took: Its overall model: Diablo began as a turn-based game based largely on Angband.
links.added: Real-time play and loot with randomly rolled magical properties.

links.took: Random dungeons and loot from the roguelikes David Brevik acknowledged.
links.added: Speed, mouse control and lavish graphics for a mainstream audience.

links.took: A deep dungeon crawl with random encounters, one of the games Brevik acknowledged.
links.added: A town hub, real-time combat and multiplayer.

links.took: Random levels, dead characters that persist, and deep, detailed rules.
links.added: A simulated world with its own history, where you manage a dwarf colony.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dwarf Fortress, citing Tarn Adams in The New York Times, 2011

links.took: Generated worlds, from a series Tarn Adams named among his main influences.
links.added: Whole world histories simulated before play begins.

links.took: A colony sim that produced stories, which amazed Tynan Sylvester.
links.added: A sci-fi colony with an AI storyteller steering events, and a friendlier interface.

links.took: Digging, building and procedurally generated worlds; Minecraft's developers cited it.
links.added: A first-person world of blocks that anyone could pick up.
links.extra: Tarn Adams has said he is thankful the Minecraft developers credited Dwarf Fortress.

links.took: A cave explorer with ropes, dynamite and a famously fragile hero.
links.added: Caves randomly generated every run, permanent death and shopkeepers who fight back.

src.t: Wikipedia: Spelunky, citing Derek Yu's book Spelunky (Boss Fight Books, 2016)

links.took: The style of an archaeologist exploring trap-filled ruins for treasure.
links.added: Short runs through randomly generated caves instead of one large hand-made ruin.

src.t: Wikipedia: Spelunky, citing Derek Yu's book Spelunky (Boss Fight Books, 2016)

links.took: Indiana Jones-style tombs full of traps and a hero who dies often.
links.added: Random levels, so memorizing trap placements no longer works.

src.t: Wikipedia: Spelunky, citing Derek Yu's book Spelunky (Boss Fight Books, 2016)

links.took: Deep interactivity, digging through walls like NetHack's pick-axe, and the temptation to rob shopkeepers.
links.added: One button to interact with anything, instead of long lists of keyboard commands.

src.t: GamesRadar+, on Derek Yu stealing from NetHack's shops as a teenager

links.took: Precise, readable platforming; Derek Yu named the Mario series one of his biggest inspirations.
links.added: Random levels and permanent death on top of that platforming.

src.t: Wikipedia: Spelunky, citing Derek Yu in Polygon, 2015

links.took: Random caves, shopkeepers, ropes, bombs and permadeath.
links.added: A Moon setting, flowing liquids, rideable mounts and online co-op.

links.took: Derek Yu and Eirik Suhrke, Spelunky's designer and composer.
links.added: Fifty new games presented as the library of a forgotten 1980s console.

links.took: Ojiro Fumoto, Downwell's creator, whose minimalist style continues in Seaside Drive.
links.added: Six developers splitting the work on fifty retro-style games.

links.took: Overhead adventuring: Pilot Quest's Wild Zone and Golfaria closely resemble the original Zelda.
links.added: A golf adventure and dozens of other genres in one collection.

links.took: Single-screen platforming against waves of enemies, in Kick Club.
links.added: One of fifty games in a collection spanning many genres.

links.took: Classic console RPG style, in Grimstone, which recalls Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy.
links.added: A complete RPG as one of fifty games.

links.took: Spelunky's run-based platforming; Ojiro Fumoto described being obsessed with it.
links.added: A vertical fall down a well, shooting with gun boots, designed for phones.

links.took: The original Zelda's dungeon layout: rooms on a grid, keys, bombs and bosses.
links.added: Random floors, permadeath and hundreds of stacking items in a dark story about religion.
links.extra: McMillen's postmortem set two goals: a roguelike built on Zelda's dungeons, and a game about his relationship with religion.

links.took: Proof that procedural generation could drive a fast action game.
links.added: Top-down shooting through randomized dungeon floors.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Binding of Isaac, citing McMillen in The Escapist, 2021

links.took: Short procedural runs that showed McMillen the potential of roguelikes.
links.added: Real-time action and a huge pool of items.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Binding of Isaac, citing The Escapist, 2021

links.took: Shooting in four directions while moving through enclosed rooms.
links.added: Tears as bullets, stat-changing items and a roguelike dungeon.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Binding of Isaac, citing VentureBeat, 2011

links.extra: McMillen compared Isaac's controls to Smash TV.

links.took: Edmund McMillen's art and dark humor; Isaac followed Super Meat Boy's success.
links.added: A switch from precision platforming to a top-down roguelike.

links.took: Rogue popularized random dungeons and permanent death, the core of Isaac's design.
links.added: Real-time shooting and short runs packed with item combinations.

links.took: Eugene Jarvis's twin-joystick arena shooting against waves of enemies.
links.added: A violent TV game show with prizes, bosses and two-player co-op.

links.took: The whole game: Isaac, items, floors and bosses.
links.added: A rebuilt engine free of Flash's limits, new pixel art, co-op and console versions.

links.took: Lessons McMillen learned making Isaac; Mewgenics' hero even has a son named Isaac.
links.added: Turn-based tactical fights and breeding generations of cats with inherited traits.

links.took: Combat modeled mainly on Pokémon battles, with each opponent tougher than the last.
links.added: Grid tactics with cats you breed between runs.

src.t: Wikipedia: Mewgenics, citing Edmund McMillen's Unboxing of Isaac stream, 2022

links.took: Tyler Glaiel, McMillen's collaborator on The End Is Nigh, and his engine.
links.added: A tactical roguelike instead of a precision platformer.

links.took: Edmund McMillen's precision platforming and grim humor.
links.added: A lone survivor after the apocalypse, collecting tumors across a connected world.

links.took: Rogue popularized randomized dungeons with permanent death.
links.added: Ten-minute puzzle dungeons where monsters stand still and exploring restores health.

links.took: Short, randomized space voyages where every trip is a new story.
links.added: Commanding one ship's crew and systems in real-time combat you can pause.

links.took: Proof that roguelike runs could work outside dungeon crawlers.
links.added: A spaceship flight across sectors with branching jumps and random events.

links.took: Subset Games' compact run-based design, by Jay Ma and Matthew Davis.
links.added: Turn-based mech tactics where every enemy attack is shown in advance.

links.took: XCOM: Enemy Unknown revived grid-based tactics, which Subset prototyped after FTL.
links.added: Tiny eight-by-eight maps, full information about enemy moves, and cities to protect.

src.t: Wikipedia: Into the Breach, citing Shacknews, 2017

links.took: A branching map of nodes with random events between fights.
links.added: Card battles and a deck built during the climb.

src.t: Wikipedia: Slay the Spire, citing Gamasutra, 2020

links.took: The founding idea: a 2D take on Demon's Souls, where death costs you.
links.added: On death, your gold passes to an heir with random traits.

src.t: Engadget, Rogue Legacy dubbed a descendant of Dark Souls 2D, 2014

links.extra: Teddy Lee said the original idea came from Demon's Souls and Dark Souls.

links.took: Demanding melee combat where dying is part of progress.
links.added: A randomized castle and permanent upgrades funded by fallen heirs.

src.t: Teddy Lee interview, Old School Gamer Magazine

links.took: Named by Teddy Lee among its main inspirations; the source doesn't say which part.
links.added: A side-scrolling castle crawl with family-line upgrades.

src.t: Teddy Lee interview, Old School Gamer Magazine

links.took: Spelunky's model for bringing roguelike design to an action genre.
links.added: Permanent upgrades between runs, making permadeath forgiving.

links.took: Heirs with random traits, a shifting castle and the manor upgrade tree.
links.added: More classes and a larger kingdom of distinct regions.

links.took: Rogue popularized turn-based random dungeons with permadeath.
links.added: Comic writing, a broad skill system and a friendlier interface.
